title: Sephardi and Mizrahi practice
hookLine: often less divided into movements, with traditional practice across a wide range
last: THE RETURN READ AS THE PROPHETS' PROMISE.

lines: A SCROLL STANDING IN ITS CASE.
cards: A tall case of carved silver stands on the reader's table. Someone unlatches it and swings it open like a cabinet, and there is the Torah scroll, upright, facing the room. The case is called a tik.
In the rows facing it sits a man who keeps every detail of Shabbat and walked here, and next to him his nephew, who drove, parked around the corner, and is singing louder than anyone.
They pray from the same book, to the tunes their families brought from far away. Nobody checks a label at the door.

teach.b: Sephardi and Mizrahi practice. You met the Sephardim on day nine hundred forty-six, and Mizrahi Jews on day nine hundred eighty-seven. Today, how they practice.
First, the names. Obadiah speaks of "the captivity of Jerusalem, which is in Sepharad."
Tradition came to read Sepharad as Spain, and Sephardi Jews trace their families to Spain and Portugal, and from there to North Africa, the Ottoman lands and beyond.

Mizrahi comes from mizrach, east, the word in the psalm's "as far as the east is from the west." Mizrahi Jews come from lands like Iraq, Iran, Yemen and Syria. The two words overlap, and families use them differently.
Second, the law. Rabbi Joseph Karo wrote the Shulchan Aruch largely following Sephardi practice. Rabbi Moses Isserles added notes for Ashkenazi Jews, printed on the same page.
One code, two customs, side by side.
Third, the movements. The split into Orthodox, Conservative, Reform and others grew up among Ashkenazi Jews in Europe and America.

Often, in Sephardi and Mizrahi communities, the synagogue stayed traditional, and people across a wide range of personal observance kept coming, without anyone needing a new label. Fourth, the custom.

teach.h: THE TORAH STANDING IN ITS CASE.
teach.b: The tik is one: carved wood in some synagogues, silver in others, the scroll inside read standing, like a book set on its spine.
Small things like that, melodies, foods, the order of prayers, carry a home across centuries and borders. The week ends here, where tradition is less a position than a house.

how: Sephardi and Mizrahi communities keep their own melodies, prayer order and customs, often following the rulings of the Shulchan Aruch, and their synagogues are frequently traditional while welcoming people of varied observance.

games.q: a Shabbat morning synagogue. a man who walked here, and his nephew who drove. who belongs in the row?
o: both, praying from the same book.
games.why: often, in Sephardi and Mizrahi communities, both: a traditional synagogue, and a wide range of observance in its rows.

practice: Picture the scroll standing upright in its case, the doors opening like a cabinet. Then bring to mind one custom from your own family, a dish, a song, a way of setting the table, that came from somewhere far away.
Hold the two side by side, and notice how a small thing carries a whole place.
